verses.translation_literal: Of David. Blessed [be] YHWH, my rock, the one who trains my hands for the fight, my fingers for the war.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David. Blessed be the LORD, my rock, who took these hands and taught them the fight, who took these fingers and schooled them for war.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a king speaking, and he does not open with his own strength: he opens with the source of it. The line is a blessing, not a request, so play it as thanksgiving from a man who has been in battle and knows his hands did not do it alone. The two halves of the verse are one thought said twice (parallelism): 'hands' and 'fingers', 'the fight' and 'the war'. Metzudat David hears exactly this: every victory comes not from the force of my hands but because the LORD trained them. Malbim goes further and splits the two: qerav is close combat, milchamah the war fought at a distance, with the bow.

The KJV has 'my strength'; the Hebrew says tsur, 'rock', the cliff you climb to escape a pursuer. Radak and Metzudat Zion gloss it as 'my strength', and the KJV follows that, but it loses the image of the mountain refuge and of a God who is solid ground. The KJV also turns 'to the fight' into the verb 'to fight' and 'to war', which hides that qerav is a noun. The headline 'a Psalm of David' is the KJV's counting; in the Hebrew the superscription is part of verse 1.

Note the participle 'the one who trains': it is continuous. This is a God who is still teaching, the way a soldier is drilled, and that is what David has to look back on.

philological_notes.note: 'My rock': the cliff or crag where a hunted man hides, and a standard title of God in the Psalms. The English versions that say 'my strength' follow the commentators' gloss rather than the word itself.
Qerav is 'battle' as a noun, and the same root means 'near': the fight at close quarters. Malbim reads it as hand-to-hand fighting against 'war' (milchamah) at range, with bow and arrow.

verses.translation_literal: My steadfast love and my stronghold, my high refuge and my rescuer, [to me] my shield, and in him I have taken refuge, the one who subdues my people under me.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is my steadfast love and my fortress, my high tower and the one who pulls me out, my shield. In him I have hidden, and he is the one who lays my people low beneath my feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The heap of nouns is the point. David does not describe God, he stacks him up, one military image on another, and each is a piece of the architecture of a besieged man: a stronghold (metsudah, a mountain fastness), a high refuge (misgav, a place so high that enemies cannot reach it), a shield for when he must fight in the open. Malbim reads them as three levels: shut inside the fort, caught on the road before reaching it, and in the open field with arrows in the air. Play it as a man naming every kind of protection he has needed.

The first word is the surprise. The KJV has 'my goodness', the ASV 'my lovingkindness'; the Hebrew is chesed, covenant love, the loyalty that binds God to his own promises, and here it stands as a title of God himself, like 'my rock'. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the name and the quality are the same thing for God. The Hebrew also has a pleonastic 'to me' after 'my rescuer'; the KJV drops it.

The last line turns from defence to rule, and it is the tension of the psalm: the God who shields him also subdues 'my people' under him (the KJV 'subdueth my people under me'). The verb radad is not the common word for 'conquer': it means to beat flat, as gold is hammered into thin sheets. The Targum, Rashi and Radak all link it to that metalwork term in Exodus 39:3. Rashi and Radak also note that 'my people' may be a defective spelling of 'peoples'. Metzudat David hears the house of Saul among the 'people'. Say it with some weight: it is a thanksgiving, but the king knows what the throne has cost.

philological_notes.note: Chesed is covenant loyalty, not 'goodness'. Said of God it names his fidelity to his promises; Meiri and Radak compare it to 'God of my praise' and 'he is your praise', where the quality stands for the one who has it.
The verb means to beat flat or hammer out, as in Exodus 39:3 where the gold is hammered into plates (Aramaic Targum rendering radidu). The picture is peoples spread flat under the king's feet.
'My people'. Rashi and Radak record that the Masoretic note lists this as a case where 'peoples' (ammim) is understood but 'ammi' is read; the translation follows the text as written.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, what [is] a human, that you know him? A son of mortal man, that you reckon him?
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD — what is a man, that you should know him? What is a mortal's child, that you should stop and reckon him?
verses.directors_commentary:
After the war-song of verses 1–2, the voice drops to a near whisper. The tone is wonder, not complaint: the king who has just boasted of his teacher and his fortress turns and asks why God should notice him at all. Psalm 8:4 asks a similar question, but it is not the same sentence. There the nouns come the other way round (enosh, then ben adam) and the verbs are 'remember' and 'visit'; here they are 'know' and 'reckon'. Read the two as cousins, not as a copy.

The verb is the heart of it. Yada' is not 'to have information about'; Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all take it as regard and favour, as in 'I have known you by name' (Exod 33:12). The KJV's 'takest knowledge of him' is serviceable but a little bureaucratic, and its closing exclamation marks turn a real question into a sigh; the Hebrew simply asks. 'Son of enosh' is a Hebrew way of saying 'a mortal, a member of the frail human kind'. Ancient readers took this as David looking back at Saul, who was king and was gone in a short time (Radak, Metzudat David).

philological_notes.note: 'And you know him', in the sense of take notice of and care for. The classical commentators gloss it as regard and favour, not as bare knowledge; the next line's 'reckon' is its partner.
'Son of mortal man'. The same pair as in Psalm 8:4, with the nouns in the opposite order there (enosh, ben adam).

verses.translation_literal: Humankind to a breath is like; his days [are] like a shadow passing.
verses.translation_dramatic: A man is a breath, a vapour on the air; his days are a shadow slipping past.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the answer to the question of verse 3 is a gesture, almost a puff of air on the stage. 'Hevel' is not an idea but a physical thing: the breath that leaves the mouth, the steam you see on a cold morning. Ecclesiastes will build a whole book on the word, and it is also the name of Abel. The KJV's 'vanity' is a Latin-flavoured abstraction ('emptiness') that has lost the picture; the BBE's 'breath' keeps it.

There is sound play in the first line: 'adam' (a human) and 'damah' (is like) share the syllable dam, so the sentence says 'man is like' with a half-echo of his own name. The second image is about time: in a land without clocks, the shadow of a wall or tree shows the hours, and it never stays still. Rashi and Meiri, citing the rabbis, prefer a shadow even faster than that, the shadow of a bird in flight (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:2), not the fixed shadow of a palm or a wall. The KJV 'passeth away' adds 'away' to a participle that just says 'passing'.

philological_notes.note: 'To a breath, to vapour'. The concrete sense is breath from the mouth; Radak and Metzudat David both compare it to the breath that leaves the mouth. The same word is Abel's name and Ecclesiastes' refrain.
'Like a passing shadow'. Rashi and Meiri, quoting the rabbis, understand the shadow of a flying bird; Radak allows either that or the shadow moving as the sun moves.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, bend down your heavens and come down; touch the mountains, and they smoke.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, bow the heavens down and come. Lay a hand on the mountains, and let them smoke.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes here. The man who sounded small now asks for the sky itself to bend, and the image is Sinai: God descending on the mountain in smoke and fire (Exodus 19:18), the thunderstorm as the divine arrival. A listener in the ancient Near East would hear the storm-god vocabulary of the neighbouring peoples, who gave Baal the lightning and the thunder; the psalm gives all of it to the LORD alone, and he does not take it as a gift but is asked to come.

The KJV 'bow thy heavens' is close to the Hebrew; it is the verb natah, 'to stretch, bend'. The verb 'touch' is gentle on purpose: a touch is enough, and the mountains smoke. Ibn Ezra's point is the logic of the verse: if a touch makes mountains smoke, what chance has a human being, who is only a breath? That is why it follows the last verse. Radak and Meiri read the mountains as kings, a metaphor; it may be, but the text gives mountains. Direct it as a plea of someone who has just admitted his own weakness.

philological_notes.note: 'Bend your heavens': the sky is thought of as a tent or vault which God can stretch down to earth. Compare 'he bowed the heavens and came down' (Psalm 18:10, as Radak himself notes).
'And they will smoke': smoke is the sign of God's presence on Sinai and of fire sent down; Radak reads it as the smoke of the burning of the wicked.

verses.translation_literal: Flash a flash of lightning and scatter them; send your arrows and confound them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Flash your lightning, LORD, and they are scattered; loose your arrows, and they run in panic.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker now asks God to fight as a storm-warrior, and the image is the ancient Near Eastern one of a heavenly archer whose arrows are lightning. It is a prayer, not a boast: the king has just asked God to come down (verse 5), and the weapons are God's, not his. The commentators read the images as figures: Radak takes lightning and arrows as 'decrees coming down from heaven', and Metzudat David takes the arrows to be thunder.

The Hebrew opens with a root repeated, 'barok baraq', 'flash a flash'. The KJV's 'Cast forth lightning' loses the echo. What the echo means is disputed. Meiri records the view that a verb joined with a noun of its own root marks intensity, as in 'bogdei bagad', but says plainly that for this verse he thinks otherwise: it means 'create a new lightning and send it to them'. Metzudat Zion simply glosses it 'send the lightning'.

The last verb is also softened or sharpened by the English. 'Hamam' is to throw into panic and confusion (Metzudat Zion derives it from mehumah, tumult); the KJV 'destroy' (and Webster's) is stronger than the Hebrew, and YLT's 'trouble' and ASV's 'discomfit' are closer. For the staging: the enemies are first scattered, then thrown into disorder, a battlefield in rout, not yet a field of corpses.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of 'to flash' with its own noun, 'flash a flash'. Meiri records the emphatic reading (as with 'bitsoa' bitsa') but himself takes it as 'create a new lightning and send it'; Ibn Ezra compares the construction to 'and he sent his arrows'; Metzudat Zion glosses 'send the lightning'.

'And you will rout them', throw them into panic. Metzudat Zion links it to mehumah, 'tumult'. The same four elements (arrows, scatter, lightning, rout) stand in Psalm 18:15, which this verse seems to echo; that is my own observation.

verses.translation_literal: Send your hands from on high; free me and deliver me from many waters, from the hand of the sons of foreignness,
verses.translation_dramatic: Reach down your hands from the height. Open a way for me, and pull me out of the deep waters, out of the grip of strangers,
verses.directors_commentary:
The request moves from the sky to a body in danger. The image is a drowning man and a rescuing hand from above. 'Many waters' is the old picture for chaos and for enemies: Ibn Ezra says it outright, that the poet compares the enemy to water, which is why the next phrase explains it ('from the hand of the sons of foreignness'). In the Near East the sea and the great waters were the powers that the storm-god defeated, so the picture connects with the storm of verses 5-6.

The KJV 'send thine hand' makes it singular; the Hebrew has the plural, 'hands'. The verb patsah is the one the KJV 'rid me' translates, a word that is not used much in modern English. Rashi gives it as 'bring me out'; Metzudat Zion and Meiri connect it with the root that means 'open', as in 'I opened my mouth' (Judges 11:35); so to rescue is to open the prison. 'Sons of foreignness' (bene nekhar) is a Hebrew idiom for foreigners; the KJV 'strange children' misleads the modern ear into thinking of children.

philological_notes.note: 'Free me': the root also means 'to open' (the mouth), so the rescue is an opening of the trap or prison.
Literally 'sons of foreignness': foreigners, outsiders. Metzudat David identifies them as idol worshippers who rose against him. 'Strange children' in the KJV is a misleading literalism.

verses.translation_literal: whose mouth speaks falsehood, and their right [hand] is a right hand of deception.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their mouths speak emptiness, and their right hands, raised in oath, are right hands of lies.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the strangers are named by their words and their hands. The mouth speaks shav, 'emptiness, falsehood'; the right hand is a 'right hand of sheqer, deception'. The right hand was the hand of oath and covenant, raised to swear or clasped to seal a bargain; so a 'right hand of deception' is a hand that lifts in a sacred oath and means nothing by it. Rashi puts it exactly that way: they stretch the right hand to swear, and swear falsely. For a modern audience the line is about treaty-breakers.

The KJV 'speaketh vanity' uses the same word, 'vanity', that it used for hevel in verse 4, so a reader loses that these are two different Hebrew words: hevel is breath, shav is the empty, the worthless. Ibn Ezra and Radak take the right hand as strength, not oath: their power is a lie. Both fit; the oath reading is stronger. Meiri and Malbim go a different way, to say that their religion itself is the false right hand, since they trust idols. Deliver it as contempt, flat and cold.

philological_notes.note: 'Emptiness, falsehood': not the breath of hevel in verse 4 but a worthless word. Rashi says shav belongs to the mouth and sheqer to the hand.
'A right hand of deception': the hand of oath, raised or clasped in a pledge that is false. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as 'strength' instead.

verses.translation_literal: O God, a new song I will sing to you; with a lyre of ten I will make music to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God — a new song I will sing to you; on the ten-stringed lyre I will make music for you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns from plea to vow. The singer has asked to be rescued and promises praise: the new song is the song for a rescue that has not happened yet. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David both place the singing after deliverance; Meiri adds that the 'new' song answers a new wonder after despair. 'Shir hadash' is a stock phrase of the psalms (compare Psalm 33:3, which also has a lyre and a new song), and a new song needs a new mercy. Note the change of name: the poem has said YHWH since verse 1 and now says 'Elohim', God, which the KJV renders 'O God' correctly.

The instrument is the problem. 'Nevel' is a large stringed instrument, a lyre or harp, and 'asor' means 'ten'. The KJV's 'a psaltery and an instrument of ten strings' counts two instruments, which follows Metzudat David, who supplies a missing waw ('with a lyre and an asor'), and probably Ibn Ezra, whose gloss runs 'with a lyre, with the ten'. A single ten-stringed lyre is the other natural reading (YLT, ASV, BBE), and Meiri has one more: a skin-like vessel with ten holes. The Hebrew as it stands says 'a lyre of ten', and I keep that. Ancient listeners would have heard it as plain as 'a twelve-string guitar'.

philological_notes.note: 'With a lyre of ten', that is a ten-stringed lyre, or, in the reading that supplies a waw, a lyre and a ten-stringed instrument. Metzudat David supplies the waw and takes 'asor' as a separate ten-stringed instrument; Ibn Ezra glosses 'with a lyre, with the ten'; Meiri takes one vessel with ten holes. Psalm 92:4 lists 'asor and nevel side by side, which is evidence for two instruments; Psalm 33:2 has 'nevel 'asor in one phrase like this verse (my own observation).
'A new song', a song for a deliverance still to come; Meiri says it answers a renewal of wonders after despair.

verses.translation_literal: the one who gives deliverance to the kings, who sets free David his servant from the sword of evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, who give victory to kings, who snatched David, your servant, from the sword of harm.
verses.directors_commentary:
The new song gets its first line here, and it is a title of God: the one who gives deliverance to kings. It is a bold thing for a king to say. Radak and Metzudat David both press the point: even kings, with their armies, depend on God for rescue. Then David names himself in the third person, 'David his servant', as if from outside, a humility that Metzudat David compares to Samuel speaking of 'Samuel' (1 Samuel 12:11). 'Servant' (eved) is a title of honour for a man who belongs to the LORD, and also a plain word for someone who is owned.

The KJV 'the hurtful sword' is a little precious; the Hebrew is 'sword of evil', that is, an evil sword, a murderous one. Which sword? Radak and Metzudat David say Saul's; Rashi relates the rescue to the rock of division, when an angel called Saul away from capturing David (1 Samuel 23). The Targum names Goliath's sword. The text is silent, so keep the sword unnamed: the audience supplies it. Notice the same verb as in verse 7: patsah, the rescue that opens. This is the God David has asked for in verse 7, and he cites his own record.

philological_notes.note: The same root as 'free me' in verse 7 and verse 11: the participle ('the one who sets free') recalls past rescue as the ground of the request.
'Sword of evil': an evil, deadly sword. The commentators name Saul's sword (Radak, Metzudat David), against the Targum's Goliath; the verse itself does not say.

verses.translation_literal: Free me and deliver me from the hand of the sons of foreignness, whose mouth speaks falsehood, and their right [hand] is a right hand of deception.
verses.translation_dramatic: Open the way for me and pull me out of the hands of strangers, whose mouths speak emptiness, whose right hands swear lies.
verses.directors_commentary:
The request comes back word for word from verses 7 and 8, the refrain of the psalm. It is the hinge: the prayer for rescue goes round again, but with the song and the record of verse 10 in between, so that it is no longer a cry of fear but a claim on a God who has done this before. Rashi puts the logic in a line: as you freed me then, free me now. Metzudat David says the same, pointing to the sword of Saul.

Meiri notes that the speaker is 'I' but means the whole people: the king speaks in the singular for all Israel. For the actor: the same words as before, said again, but slower, with the weight of what has happened between. The KJV 'rid me' and 'strange children' are the same as before, and the repeat of the whole of verse 8 shows that the poem is circling, not moving on.

philological_notes.note: The pair of verbs is the same as in verse 7: 'free' (open) and 'deliver' (pull out). The refrain returns after the song.

verses.translation_literal: Which [are] our sons like saplings, grown great in their youth; our daughters like corners, hewn, the pattern of a palace.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then our sons will stand like saplings, tall and thriving in their youth; and our daughters like corner-pillars, shaped and fitted, the very pattern of a palace.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood shifts at once from enemies to home, and from fear to a picture of blessing. The verse has no verb: it opens with 'asher' and two verbless comparisons, so every English version has to decide what kind of sentence it is. The KJV and Webster turn it into a prayer ('that our sons may be'); ASV says 'when'; YLT states it as fact ('because our sons are'). Rashi takes it as a present boast about this generation; Meiri as a prophecy of redemption. Keep the staging open, a hope that sounds like a certainty.

In the ancient world children were the farm's labour and the household's old-age pension, so sons 'grown great in their youth' are strength: saplings that the owner watered and that stand tall early (Radak, Meiri; Malbim adds the lesson that a sapling must be trained straight). Daughters are 'like corners', the dressed stones at the angles of a great building, 'hewn' to match so precisely that the corner looks like one block (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David), 'the pattern of a palace', a word that also means a temple. The KJV supplies 'stones' and 'polished', where the Hebrew has only 'corners' and 'hewn' (a word for cutting wood or stone). The same word for corners, zaviyyot, appears in Zechariah 9:15, 'like the corners of the altar', and Rashi records a rabbinic reading (Pesachim 87a) that takes it from there, as daughters filled with passion like altar corners filled with blood, meaning that they belong only to their husbands. Others, such as Metzudat David, hear modesty and uprightness, nothing crooked in them.

philological_notes.note: 'Like corners'. The word is used of building corners and, in Zechariah 9:15, of altar corners ('like the corners of the altar'), which is the link the rabbis follow in Rashi's report of Pesachim 87a. Rashi and Meiri otherwise take the picture as stone corners that line up as one piece; Ibn Ezra hears a palace that is carved and adorned.

'Hewn, cut'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare 'chatuvot 'etun Mitzrayim' (Proverbs 7:16); Metzudat Zion compares 'mechotev etzekha' (Deuteronomy 29:10), the cutter of wood. The KJV 'polished' goes beyond the root.
'The pattern of a palace'. Heikhal is a great house, a king's palace or a temple; Ibn Ezra reads the phrase as a repetition of the sense already given.

verses.translation_literal: Our granaries [are] full, supplying from kind to kind; our flock bearing thousands, bearing ten-thousands, in our open places.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our storehouses full to the corners, giving out kind after kind; our flocks bearing thousands, tens of thousands, out in the open streets.
verses.directors_commentary:
From sons and daughters the poem passes to barn and field. Radak and Meiri both notice that the three blessings of the psalm (children, the produce of the soil, and flocks) follow Deuteronomy 28:4, 'blessed shall be the fruit of your womb, the fruit of your ground and the fruit of your livestock'. The singer is asking for the covenant blessings as they stand in the Torah, and the stage picture is a village that lacks nothing.

Two words are hard. 'Mezavenu' is rare; Rashi, Radak and Meiri hear 'our corners' (zaviyyot) and picture grain stored in one corner of the house per kind, so the word echoes the corners of verse 12, while the sense 'our granaries' is the usual one. 'Mi-zan el zan' is either 'from kind to kind', all sorts of grain (Targum, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri), or 'from one harvest to the next', provision to last the year (Rashi, Metzudat David, and 'some say' in Meiri). The KJV's 'all manner of store' takes the first reading and loses the doubt.

The flocks show a sound play: 'ma'alifot' and 'merubbavot' are verbs made from 'thousand' and 'ten thousand', so the sheep 'thousand' and 'ten-thousand'; the KJV's 'bring forth thousands and ten thousands' keeps the sense but not the made-up verbs. 'Hutzot' is the open space outside the house, so 'streets' is right for a town, and the ASV's and BBE's 'fields' fits the pasture reading. Note also the unusual spelling of 'tzo'nenu' with an extra aleph.

philological_notes.note: A rare word for 'granaries'. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion link it to zaviyyot, 'corners', and picture each kind of grain kept in its own corner.
'From kind to kind' (Targum's 'lezanohi', 'to its kind'; Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) or 'from harvest to harvest', that is from one year to the next (Rashi, Metzudat David).
Verbs made from 'thousand' and 'ten-thousand': 'thousanding, ten-thousanding'. Radak and Ibn Ezra take them as bearing young to the thousand and ten-thousand.

verses.translation_literal: Our oxen [are] loaded; [there is] no breach and no going out and no outcry in our wide squares.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our oxen go heavy under their load. No wall is broken, no one is led out through a gap, and in our wide squares there is no cry of alarm. Only the creak of the yoke, and the quiet.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood turns from abundance to safety, and the voice should drop. The oxen (alluphenu) are the heavy animals of the village, the engine of its ploughing and hauling, and the word is the same root as the 'thousand' of verse 13 and as 'clan chief' (alluf): Rashi hears it as 'our chiefs, carried by the small ones who obey them', so a listener of his day might hear both. 'Loaded' (mesubbalim) is read as strength (they carry wagons, Ibn Ezra, Radak) or as fatness, so well fed that they bear their own flesh (Meiri, Metzudat David); the KJV's 'strong to labour' picks the first and adds 'that they may', which is not in the Hebrew. The three negatives are the real drama: peretz is a breach in a city wall (Ibn Ezra), the point where an attacker enters; yotzet is 'going out', which the commentators take as captives marched off into exile (Radak, Metzudat David), but the feminine form is also the word used for a premature birth, and that is how the BBE reads it ('our cows give birth safely'), which sits well with a verse about cattle. The KJV's 'nor going out' keeps the uncertainty; it does not choose. Tsevachah is not 'complaining', as the KJV has it, but a shriek of distress in public, the cry that goes up when a city is hit (Jer 14:2 uses the same word of Jerusalem). Ibn Ezra adds that it was the custom for news of defeat to be cried in the squares, and Radak notes that this never happened under David. The rechovot are the broad open spaces inside the gate where the city meets, trades and judges: if no one is screaming there, the town is safe. Play it as relief, not as boasting.

philological_notes.note: 'Our oxen' (Radak, Metzudat Zion, citing Deut 7:13 'the offspring of your cattle'); the same root gives alluf 'chief'. Rashi alone takes it as 'our chiefs'.
A breach, such as one made in a city wall; Ibn Ezra specifies the walls of the city. Metzudat David extends it to a breach in the people and the herd.
Feminine participle 'going out': of captives (Radak), of a soul outside the proper bounds (Meiri), or in the sense of a miscarriage. Unsettled.
A loud cry of distress, in a time of calamity; Metzudat Zion compares Jer 14:2, 'the cry (tsevachah) of Jerusalem has gone up'.

verses.translation_literal: Blessednesses of the people that thus [it is] to it; blessednesses of the people that YHWH [is] its God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy the people for whom it is so: the oxen laden, the walls whole, the squares without alarm. Happy, happy the people whose God is the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two lines, one beat apart, and the second answers the first. The song has just painted a whole world in the plural: sons like grown saplings, daughters like carved corner pillars, full granaries, flocks in their tens of thousands, oxen heavy with load, no breach and no cry in the squares. Now the speaker steps back and says what to make of it. Play the first line as a gesture at all of that: 'such is it for them.' Play the second as the reason. The old readers saw this plainly. Ibn Ezra asks why all this good has come to the people and answers: because the LORD is their God. Radak says the same, that the people have this success because the LORD is their God, and therefore they are fortunate. Malbim goes a step further and reads the second line as the chief happiness, the one that the rest flows from. Metzudat David takes the God of the people as the one whose hand does not fall short in giving good. Rashi on the first line is brief: all this good is theirs.

The KJV 'Happy' flattens אַשְׁרֵי, which is a plural construct, literally 'the blessednesses of', an exclamation that piles up as it is said; the Psalter opens with the same word (Psalm 1:1). The KJV 'that is in such a case' is a stiff, archaic stand-in for the plain Hebrew 'that thus [it is] to it', and the ASV copies it. The relative שֶׁ, instead of the usual אֲשֶׁר, is a mark of the later, spoken-sounding Hebrew of these final Psalms, so the line should sound like speech and not like a formula. The same שֶׁ is joined to the divine name in שֶׁיְהוָה, a compact 'that-YHWH', which the KJV opens out into 'whose God is the Lord'.

philological_notes.note: Plural construct of 'esher, 'blessedness, good fortune': 'O the blessednesses of'. It is an exclamation of congratulation on a state already enjoyed, not a wish. Metzudat Zion glosses it as an expression of praise, like 'ashrei ha'ish' in Psalm 1.
A verbless clause: the relative שֶׁ, the adverb 'thus' and 'to it'. 'Thus' points back to the blessings just listed in the psalm. Rashi reads it as 'all this good is theirs'.
